judge_assessment.explanation: Confirmed exactly, including the mechanism. worksheet.pdf problem 7 prints two labelled parts in this order: '(a) Write cos A as an exact fraction in lowest terms:' then '(b) Find angle A:'. answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '7. 21.79, 13/14'. The correct values are cos A = (100 + 196 - 36)/(2 x 10 x 14) = 260/280 = 13/14 and A = arccos(13/14) = 21.79 degrees, so the two printed numbers are right but sit in the wrong slots. The cause is that verify.json id 7 lists its triangle entry (expected 21.79) before its eval entry (expected '13/14'), and scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry joins expected values in verify.json array order with no reference to the printed part order and no labels. The neighbouring multi-part rows happen to be correct only because their entries were declared in prompt order — problem 5 declares side then area and prints '17.29, 50.74', problem 11 declares c then A and prints '24.05, 50.58'. So this is one array ordering away from being wrong on any multi-part item, and it was wrong here. The judge's other claims hold too: I recomputed all twelve results independently (7.24, 95.74, 9.24, 45.21, 17.29 with area 50.74, 55.86, 13/14 and 21.79, 36.28, 121.03, 59.49, 24.05 with 50.58, 37.36) and every one matches the key to the stated two-decimal rounding, so mathematical_correctness 2 reflects the answer-key mismatch rather than any computational error. Problem 12's manual reasoning item does correctly explain why the law of sines cannot start an SAS problem. Beyond the judge's finding I note a second, uncounted open response: problem 11(b) instructs 'say which you chose and why', and verify.json id 11 carries two triangle entries and no manual entry, so the sheet prints two written-reasoning requests and declares one.

strengths_to_preserve: Every problem carries its own TikZ figure showing only that problem's givens with a '?' on the unknown, and the worksheet directions state the labelling convention once ('side a is opposite vertex A ...') so the figures do not have to re-explain it. For SAS/SSS work, where the commonest error is putting the wrong side opposite the named angle, the per-problem figure is the right investment.

Problem 2's key makes the topic's key structural point: 'A negative cosine means an obtuse angle, and the inverse cosine returns it directly (no ambiguity, unlike the law of sines).' That is exactly why the law of cosines is the tool for SSS, and it is stated where the student meets the first negative cosine rather than saved for the summary.

Problem 1's key closes with a sanity check tied to the figure — 'The answer is shorter than both given sides, which is right for an angle under 60 degrees squeezed between them' — matching the directions' instruction to check every answer against the figure. The habit is taught by demonstration on the very first item.

The common-wrong-answers block names the mechanism, not just the number: 14.41 from 'a plus sign in front of the 2ab cosine term', 32.16 from 'the wrong side opposite the angle', and 95 from 'added the two distances instead of using the law of cosines'. The last is the characteristic navigation-problem error and is worth keeping on any bearings item.

The difficulty ramp does what the prompt asked without repeating a skeleton: SAS, SSS, SAS with rotated letters, SSS in context, SAS plus area, a bearings problem, an exact-fraction cosine, an obtuse included angle, a navigation turn, a Heronian 13-14-15 triangle, a two-part solve where the student chooses the second law, and a context problem with a written justification.

Problem 7 asking for cos A as an exact fraction BEFORE the decimal angle is good pedagogy — it forces the student to see 260/280 reduce to 13/14 rather than reaching for arccos immediately. The defect is in how the bank printed it, not in the item.

root_causes.description: The Quick Answers bank concatenates a problem's expected values in verify.json array order and prints them unlabelled, so the mapping from value to printed sub-part depends entirely on the order the author happened to declare entries. Problem 7's entries are declared angle-first, part (a) asks for the cosine, and the row silently inverts the two answers. Nothing in the pipeline compares the bank's value order against the worksheet's (a)/(b) order, which is why gate_log reports the answer-key gates green.
evidence: verify.json id 7 entry order: {"type": "triangle", given {a:6,b:10,c:14}, expected 21.79} then {"type": "eval", expr '(b**2 + c**2 - a**2)/(2*b*c)', expected '13/14'}.
worksheet.pdf problem 7 part order: (a) cos A as an exact fraction, (b) angle A.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry: 'vals = [e["expected"] for e in entries ...]; text = ", ".join(_fmt(v) for v in vals)' — array order, no labels, no cross-check against the prompt.
Rows 5 and 11 are correct only incidentally: their entries were declared in the same order the prompt asks for them.

root_causes.description: Problem 11(b) prints a written-reasoning request — after computing angle A the student must 'say which you chose and why' — and verify.json id 11 contains only two triangle entries. The package therefore declares one manual item (problem 12(b)) when the worksheet prints two open responses, and the judge reviewed one.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 11: 'Once you have all three sides, you may use either law for part (b) — say which you chose and why.'
verify.json id 11: two triangle entries (expected 24.05 and 50.58), no manual entry.
verify.json id 12 does carry a manual entry, so the mechanism was available and simply not applied to 11.

root_causes.description: Problem 12 mixes a machine entry with its declared manual entry, and the bank row shows no manual marker because render_entry reaches the '---' fallback only when a problem has no machine-expected values at all. The one item the author correctly flagged for hand review looks finished in the grading column.
evidence: verify.json id 12: a triangle entry (expected 37.36) plus a manual entry for part (b).
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers row: '12. 37.36', with no marker.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry: the manual em-dash is guarded by 'if not vals'.

improvements.title: Bind each Quick Answers value to its printed sub-part label instead of relying on verify.json array order
improvements.proposed_change: Add a required 'slot' field to any verify entry belonging to a problem with more than one entry — the sub-part label as printed ('a', 'b', or a short caption such as 'cos A'). scripts/render_quick_answers.py then emits labelled values in the worksheet's part order rather than the JSON array's order, e.g. '7. (a) cos A = 13/14; (b) A = 21.79 deg'. Add a check to tests/check_answer_key.py that extracts the (a)/(b)/(c) markers from the worksheet source for each problem and fails when the number of bank values differs from the number of parts or when a declared slot is missing, so an ordering mistake becomes a build failure instead of a printed error. Raising this above the p2 the key normally carries is deliberate: unlabelled values are confusing, but reordered values are wrong, and this case shows the two failure modes are the same bug.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture reproducing curr-427 problem 7: a two-part prompt asking (a) for cos A and (b) for angle A, with verify.json declaring the angle entry first and the cosine entry second. Assert the rendered bank row reads '(a) 13/14; (b) 21.79' — i.e. prompt order with labels — and NOT the current '21.79, 13/14'. Add a negative case where a two-part prompt has entries carrying no slot field and assert the gate fails.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes this case's hard failure directly, and removes the latent version of it from every other multi-part row in the suite, which today is correct only when the author's declaration order happens to match the printed order. Also fixes the unlabelled-value complaint the key was originally cut for (curr-334's 'AC and BD' row).
improvements.risk: Requires a slot field on existing verify.json files or a migration that infers slots from order, and inference reintroduces the very assumption being removed — so the inference path must be a one-time migration with author review, not a permanent fallback. Labelled rows are also wider and will reduce the bank's adaptive column count on dense sheets.

improvements.title: Declare problem 11(b)'s 'say which you chose and why' as a manual sub-part
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual verify entry for any printed request whose answer is a sentence, including when it is attached to a computed part of the same problem. Enforce it by scanning worksheet prompt text for justification imperatives ('say which ... and why', 'explain why ...', 'say what ...') and failing the gate when the matching verify id has no manual entry. references/manual-review-aid.md should carry the method-choice pattern explicitly: asking a student to justify a tool choice is a reasoning item even when the number that precedes it is machine-checked.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture from curr-427 problem 11: a two-part prompt whose trailing sentence is 'say which you chose and why', with a verify id containing only triangle entries. The gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged justification and pass once a manual entry is added; assert the fixture's reported manual count rises from 1 to 2.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the manual-item count match what the worksheet actually prints. On procedural-fluency sheets a trailing 'and say why' is a common way to add depth without adding an item, and it is currently invisible to the verification contract.
improvements.risk: Text scanning over-triggers on instructional asides and under-triggers on justifications phrased as questions; the lint needs an author override and should be tuned against existing baseline worksheets before hard-failing.

improvements.title: Show a manual-review marker on Quick Answers rows that mix machine and manual entries
improvements.proposed_change: Change scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry so any problem whose entry list contains a type == 'manual' appends an explicit marker to its bank row, instead of reaching the em-dash only when the problem has no machine entries. Add a one-line legend beneath the bank so a printed key explains its own glyph.
improvements.regression_test: Render curr-427's verify.json id 12 (one triangle entry expected 37.36 plus one manual entry) and assert the bank row carries a manual marker. It renders today as a bare '37.36', so the assertion fails before the fix; assert a manual-only problem still renders the plain em-dash.
improvements.expected_impact: Surfaces the sheet's declared reasoning item in the column a teacher grades from. Combined with the previous fix it means both of this worksheet's written responses become visible rather than one being invisible and the other undeclared.
improvements.risk: Extra row width can reduce the adaptive column count; use a single glyph rather than a word.

case_summary: A mathematically clean law-of-cosines fluency set — I recomputed all twelve results and every one matches the key at the stated rounding, including the exact fraction 13/14 and the Heronian 13-14-15 angle. Each problem carries its own figure with only its givens and a '?' on the unknown, the ramp never repeats a skeleton, and the key teaches the structural reason the law of cosines is the SSS tool ('a negative cosine means an obtuse angle, and the inverse cosine returns it directly — no ambiguity, unlike the law of sines'). The REJECT rests on one printed row and the judge's diagnosis is exact: problem 7 asks (a) for cos A and (b) for angle A, and the bank prints '21.79, 13/14'. The cause is that render_quick_answers.py joins expected values in verify.json array order with no labels and no comparison against the printed part order, and this problem's entries were declared angle-first. Rows 5 and 11 are correct only because their declaration order coincided with their prompt order, so the same bug is latent across the suite. Two smaller findings the judge did not count: problem 11(b) prints a second written-reasoning request ('say which you chose and why') that is not declared manual, and problem 12's correctly declared manual part leaves no marker in the bank.
